entities.name: René de Prie
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
René de Prie (1451–1519) emerged as a pivotal, if controversial, figure in early 16th-century French ecclesiastical politics, serving as a Roman Catholic cardinal and bishop whose career was deeply intertwined with the shifting alliances and power struggles between the French monarchy and the Papacy during the Italian Wars. Born into the influential Prie family, he was appointed Bishop of Bayeux in 1498 and later elevated to the cardinalate by Pope Julius II in 1506, a strategic move by the pontiff to secure French support, which ultimately proved fragile.

De Prie's most notable, and indeed infamous, involvement came with his prominent role in the schismatic Council of Pisa (1511) and later Milan, convened by King Louis XII of France in opposition to Pope Julius II. As a leading cardinal within this assembly, he actively participated in the deposition of Julius II, an act that led to his own excommunication by the legitimate Pope in October 1511. This bold defiance underscored the profound tensions between secular rulers seeking to control national churches and the universal authority claimed by the Roman pontiff, a conflict that defined much of the late medieval and early modern period.

Following the death of Julius II in 1513 and the ascension of Pope Leo X, René de Prie sought reconciliation with the Holy See. He was absolved of his excommunication and restored to his cardinalatial dignity in 1513, demonstrating the Papacy's pragmatic need to mend fences with powerful French figures. His career thus serves as a microcosm of the intricate diplomatic maneuvering and the often-blurred lines between political expediency and religious loyalty that characterized the era, leaving a legacy of a church grappling with internal dissent and external pressures from burgeoning nation-states.

entities.summary:
René de Prie (1451–1519) was a French Roman Catholic bishop and cardinal. Born in Touraine, he rose to prominence during the Renaissance era, earning a position as cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Minerva. De Prie played a key role in the governance of the Catholic Church, participating in several conclaves that elected popes.

As a high-ranking cleric, de Prie was involved in various diplomatic missions and negotiations with European monarchs. He also contributed to the development of ecclesiastical laws and practices, reflecting his influence on the Catholic Church's hierarchy.

De Prie's legacy extends beyond his tenure as bishop; he is remembered for his service to the Catholic Church and his role in shaping its governance during a pivotal moment in European history.

The 'Council of Trent' (1545–1563), which de Prie participated in, had far-reaching consequences for the Catholic Church and Europe as a whole. This council marked a significant turning point in the Church's response to the Protestant Reformation, aiming to reform its practices and doctrine in light of the new theological debates.

The 'Concordat of Bologna' (1519), which de Prie signed, established a framework for the relationship between the Catholic Church and the Italian city-states. This concordat had significant implications for the balance of power in Italy during the Renaissance period.

De Prie's relationships with other prominent figures of his time are also noteworthy. He collaborated with figures like Cardinal Charles de Bourbon (later King Charles IX of France), who played a crucial role in the French monarchy's rise to prominence.
